common_name: Red Charm Peony (Deep Crimson-Red Bomb-Form Exhibition Peony)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Red Charm is a benchmark bomb-form exhibition peony in deep crimson-red.

directions: Plant roots with the eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and stake the strong stems before the massive blooms open. Red Charm bears large, tightly domed bomb-form flowers in deep, velvety crimson-red, the rounded petaloid center rising from a ring of broader outer guard petals, a classic exhibition form that has made it a benchmark red peony among collectors and breeders since its introduction. Divide congested clumps only when necessary, since peonies resent disturbance and may sulk for a year or two after transplanting.

common_name: Le Cygne Peony (Renowned French Pure White Heirloom Peony)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Le Cygne, French for 'the swan,' is a legendary early-1900s French heirloom with pure white, loosely double blooms.

directions: Plant roots with the eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and stake the strong stems before the massive blooms open. Le Cygne, French for 'the swan,' carries large, loosely double, pure white flowers with a subtle ivory glow at the center, considered by many peony historians to be one of the finest white peonies ever introduced and a foundational parent behind many later white cultivars. Its refined form and near-legendary reputation have kept it prized among peony collectors for over a century. Divide congested clumps only when necessary, since peonies resent disturbance and may sulk for a year or two after transplanting.

common_name: Nick Shaylor Peony (Bomb-Form Blush Pink Fading to Cream)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Nick Shaylor is a classic bomb-form double peony in blush pink fading to creamy white.

directions: Plant roots with the eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and stake the strong stems before the massive blooms open. Nick Shaylor bears large, tightly domed bomb-form flowers that open a soft blush pink and gradually fade to creamy white as they mature, giving a single planting a gentle gradient of color over its bloom period, opening from broad outer guard petals surrounding the rounded petaloid center typical of the bomb form. Divide congested clumps only when necessary, since peonies resent disturbance and may sulk for a year or two after transplanting.

common_name: Shirley Temple Peony (Fragrant Double Fading Soft Pink to Near-White)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Shirley Temple is a fragrant double peony opening soft pink and fading to near-white.

directions: Plant roots with the eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and stake the strong stems before the massive blooms open. Shirley Temple bears large, fully double flowers with a strong, sweet fragrance, opening a soft pale pink and fading to nearly white as the bloom matures, giving a single planting a gentle gradient of color over its bloom period. Its fragrance and classic double form have made it a long-standing favorite for cutting and for scenting a spring garden. Divide congested clumps only when necessary, since peonies resent disturbance and may sulk for a year or two after transplanting.

common_name: Paula Fay Peony (Early-Blooming Bright Coral-Pink Semi-Double)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Paula Fay is an early-blooming semi-double peony with bright coral-pink flowers on a vigorous landscape plant.

directions: Plant roots with the eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Paula Fay bears bright, clear coral-pink, semi-double flowers with a ring of golden stamens visible at the open center, blooming notably early in the peony season, which extends the flowering window when paired with later-blooming cultivars. The vigorous, floriferous plant is a strong landscape performer valued as much for its garden presence as for cut flowers. Divide congested clumps only when necessary, since peonies resent disturbance and may sulk for a year or two after transplanting.

common_name: Coral Sunset Peony (Semi-Double Fading Coral-Peach to Cream)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Coral Sunset opens coral-peach and fades to soft cream, an unusual warm color rare among peony cultivars.

directions: Plant roots with the eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Coral Sunset bears semi-double flowers that open a warm coral-peach and gradually fade to soft cream as they mature, an unusual warm color rare among peony cultivars that are more typically found in shades of pink, red, and white. Its distinctive coloring has made it one of the most sought-after and widely imitated peony introductions of its era. Divide congested clumps only when necessary, since peonies resent disturbance and may sulk for a year or two after transplanting.

common_name: Gay Paree Peony (Japanese-Form Rose-Pink with Ruffled Cream Center)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Gay Paree is a Japanese-form peony with rose-pink guard petals surrounding a ruffled creamy-white center.

directions: Plant roots with the eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Gay Paree bears a striking Japanese-form flower, a single ring of broad, rose-pink guard petals surrounding a dense, ruffled mass of narrower creamy-white staminodes at the center, a lighter, more textured bloom than the fully double bomb form and highly attractive to bees since the flower's structure remains more open. Its two-tone contrast has made it one of the most recognizable and widely planted Japanese-form peonies. Divide congested clumps only when necessary, since peonies resent disturbance and may sulk for a year or two after transplanting.

common_name: Big Ben Peony (Full Double Deep Maroon-Red Late-Season Peony)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Big Ben is a full double peony in deep maroon-red, a vigorous late-season bloomer.

directions: Plant roots with the eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and stake the strong stems before the massive blooms open. Big Ben bears large, full double flowers in deep, dramatic maroon-red, blooming late in the peony season, which extends the flowering window into a period when many earlier peonies have finished. Its dark, saturated color and vigorous, robust plant make it a strong anchor for the back of a peony border. Divide congested clumps only when necessary, since peonies resent disturbance and may sulk for a year or two after transplanting.

common_name: Cora Stubbs Peony (Japanese-Form Rose-Pink with Pink-and-Cream Center)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Cora Stubbs is a Japanese-form peony with rose-pink outer petals and pink-and-cream staminodes.

directions: Plant roots with the eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Cora Stubbs bears a Japanese-form flower, a ring of broad, rose-pink guard petals surrounding a dense center of narrower staminodes blended pink and cream, a softer, more textured center than the vivid contrast of Gay Paree, and highly attractive to bees since the flower's structure remains more open than a fully double bloom. Its refined color combination has made it a popular choice among peony collectors. Divide congested clumps only when necessary, since peonies resent disturbance and may sulk for a year or two after transplanting.

common_name: Angel Cheeks Peony (Fragrant Bomb-Type Soft Blush Pink)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Angel Cheeks is a fragrant bomb-type double peony in soft blush pink.

directions: Plant roots with the eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and stake the strong stems before the massive blooms open. Angel Cheeks bears large, tightly domed bomb-form flowers in soft, gentle blush pink with a sweet fragrance, the rounded petaloid center rising from a ring of broader outer guard petals in the classic bomb form. Its soft color and fragrance make it a favorite for cutting and for scenting a spring garden. Divide congested clumps only when necessary, since peonies resent disturbance and may sulk for a year or two after transplanting.

common_name: Top Brass Peony (Bomb-Form Cream with Butter-Yellow Center)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Top Brass opens cream with a butter-yellow center that fades to ivory.

directions: Plant roots with the eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and stake the strong stems before the massive blooms open. Top Brass bears large, tightly domed bomb-form flowers that open cream with a distinct butter-yellow blush at the center, gradually fading to soft ivory as the bloom matures, giving a single planting a gentle gradient of color. The rounded petaloid center rises from a ring of broader outer guard petals in the classic bomb form. Divide congested clumps only when necessary, since peonies resent disturbance and may sulk for a year or two after transplanting.

common_name: Bowl of Cream Peony (Large Pure Ivory-White Bomb-Type Double)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Bowl of Cream is a large bomb-type double peony with pure ivory-white petals.

directions: Plant roots with the eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and stake the strong stems before the massive blooms open. Bowl of Cream bears exceptionally large, tightly domed bomb-form flowers in pure ivory-white, one of the largest and most impressive white peony cultivars widely grown, the rounded petaloid center rising from a ring of broad outer guard petals in the classic bomb form. Its imposing size and clean color have kept it a favorite among peony collectors and exhibitors for decades. Divide congested clumps only when necessary, since peonies resent disturbance and may sulk for a year or two after transplanting.

common_name: Command Performance Peony (Full Double Vivid Coral-Pink)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Command Performance is a full double peony in vivid coral-pink with a strong upright habit.

directions: Plant roots with the eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and stake the strong stems before the massive blooms open. Command Performance bears large, full double flowers in vivid, saturated coral-pink on an especially strong, upright plant that holds its heavy blooms well without excessive flopping, an advantage over some floppier double peony cultivars. Its bright color and sturdy habit have made it a reliable choice for both garden display and cutting. Divide congested clumps only when necessary, since peonies resent disturbance and may sulk for a year or two after transplanting.

common_name: Julia Rose Itoh Peony (Semi-Double Fading Red-Orange to Peach to Yellow)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Julia Rose is an Itoh (intersectional) hybrid whose semi-double blooms open deep red-orange and fade through peach to soft yellow.

directions: Plant roots with the eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Julia Rose, an Itoh (intersectional) hybrid combining traits of herbaceous and tree peonies, bears semi-double flowers that open a deep red-orange and gradually fade through peach to soft yellow as they age, giving a single planting a striking gradient of warm colors rarely seen in straight herbaceous peony cultivars. Itoh hybrids have sturdier stems that hold up blooms without staking and often rebloom lightly, along with better disease resistance than many lactiflora cultivars. Unlike tree peonies, Itoh hybrids die back to the ground each winter like herbaceous types.

common_name: First Arrival Itoh Peony (Large Lavender-Pink Semi-Double)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; First Arrival is one of the earliest-released Itoh hybrids, bearing large lavender-pink semi-double blooms.

directions: Plant roots with the eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. First Arrival, one of the earliest Itoh (intersectional) hybrids ever released, bears large, semi-double flowers in soft lavender-pink with a ring of golden stamens visible at the open center, combining the strong stems and repeat-flowering tendency of Itoh hybrids with a classic soft peony color. Its early introduction and reliable performance helped establish Itoh hybrids as a mainstream peony class distinct from herbaceous and tree types. Unlike tree peonies, Itoh hybrids die back to the ground each winter like herbaceous types, and their sturdy stems hold up blooms without staking.
